items.ownerFullName: Morgan Graffis | Cleaning Business Coach | Hiring & Growth
items.transcript: If you are in purgatory, yeah, I'm calling it purgatory, okay? If you're in purgatory in your cleaning company and you are so good at cleaning and you keep getting clients, but you max out your schedule and all of a sudden you're like, oh, like I'm going to grow this thing, I'm going to start a team, but you actually cannot find a good cleaner to save your life. Or when you do find somebody that you're excited about, it's like one weekend and you start getting complaints from your clients because the cleaner ended up not being as good as you thought they were going to be or like your training system isn't as good as you thought it was going to be. Okay, first of all, welcome to my life for literally three years. It was, I thought about quitting every single day. I was just stubborn and I didn't want to work a nine to five. So I kept going even though it was really, really bad and I would consistently hire people and it would consistently go wrong and it was just a nightmare. So I'm going to share a couple things that have definitely helped that I've created. It's been what, six years since I started my cleaning company, a little over six years now. I've sold it and before I sold it, I was able to sell it because I had all of these little like systems in place. So I want to share what worked. This is getting into the weeds a little bit and I don't want you to click off because you're not understanding because it's really not that complicated, but I shoot for a 70% capacity rate, meaning I only book up 70% of our schedule and I leave 30% as buffer. So if you're in dreaded purgatory and you're like, oh my God, I'm understaffed. Like, I don't know. If literally one thing goes wrong, like the whole entire schedule falls apart and then you're working until like 10 PM cleaning house or like, you know, it's really bad. I don't allow that to happen because of the buffer built into my schedule. Like I literally will not book over 70%. I'll instead start a wait list. And really what I call the runway is 60 to 70% capacity. So when I'm hitting 60% capacity, that's my trigger to be onboarding more cleaners. Number two is just interview more people. Just interview people all the time. Have somebody in your business who is in charge of interviewing people literally all the time. Number three is a training system. I know saying a training system literally gives you no information at all. So if you would like my training system, like a little mini guide on how to create your own, you can just comment like training system or something and I'll send you like a little mini guide. But yeah, having that training system in place, life changing. Definitely recommend having a system of training in place and having people on site, not just one person, but somebody on site on every single clean who is in charge of making sure that training system is getting done for the newbies and making sure that quality control is done for not only the newbies, but also the people on your team who are out of training because they need to be checked too.

items.transcript: We do that for a couple reasons. So when I was transitioning out of walkthroughs and I ended up delegating that task, something that I noticed was if the person who did the walkthroughs wasn't on the first clean, things would get missed, like major things. So for some reason, we were just not really giving the right information to our administrative assistant to then pass along to the cleaning team. So it was like the game of telephone. We're like, okay, the general manager was doing the walkthroughs. That walkthrough would then need to get transferred over to our administrative assistant who would do like all the back end stuff on Java or create the client portal, et cetera. And then the cleaners would be the ones on site, but maybe the GM wasn't there. Maybe they were, right? When the GM wasn't there or whoever was doing our walkthrough, sometimes it was even me back in the day. If I wasn't on site after I'd done a walkthrough, maybe it's the case that there's an entire level that we miss when we're on site because the cleaners think that we're skipping that area. But in reality, you know, when I did the walkthrough, they confirmed that they wanted the basement. Things like that would happen all the time. And that's a super unfortunate thing because that's, you know, the first clean is when you're really trying to prove to the client that you're a professional, that you have everything organized, that you can provide super high quality. Obviously, if you miss an entire floor of a house or maybe you miss a room because the door is closed or something, that's not good. It's not going to create a good relationship with that client. And they're likely probably not going to book with you again. And if they do, they're already feeling that like reservation to do so. And you don't want that. You want after that first clean for them to be a raving fan. So when we started implementing the video, whoever was on site doing the walkthrough, which was never our admin because our admin worked totally remote, we would have that video sent to our admin to then save on file. So when our admin is building out our job forms, which is essentially like our customized checklist for that client that is custom for that home, so it literally lists the rooms in that home, they're able to look at the video to make sure that no rooms and no areas of the house were missed. items.caption:
How do you manage your small business finances? Are you randomly moving money over when you “need it” 😝 you might think about trying this instead 💕

#cleaning #cleaningcompany #cleaningtipsandtricks
items.ownerFullName: Morgan Graffis | Cleaning Business Coach | Hiring & Growth
items.transcript: These are the allocations that I have for my cleaning company that work the best for me. So what do we actually do with these allocations? I feel like when I was first reading Profit First, I was like, okay, so we decide on certain percentages and now what? Is the money just gonna come like from thin air? So this is the tactical part that you need to immediately put into place. These allocations are going to turn into bank accounts for you. So right now you might have one business account. Let's just say you have currently one business account. We'll just call that biz account, okay? So that's where all of your money comes in and that's where all of your money comes out. So anytime you're getting money from a client or maybe you're getting a loan or maybe any type of money going in comes into that account. Then you're paying yourself, maybe you're paying your contractors, maybe you're paying your employees, maybe you're buying vacuums, maybe you're buying any type of supplies, your storage unit, any of your subscriptions, all of it comes out of this account. Now, the tactical thing that you get to do right after watching this is to separate that into different bank accounts. So you're going to walk into your bank and you're going to say, I need five separate accounts for my business. So you're going to tell them I need a account for profit, an account for operating expenses, an account for payroll, an account for taxes, and an account for owner's draw. You're going to make it to where the funds get transferred to this revenue account. So when you get this money in here, you're going to have a day that you do all of your allocations. So you're not gonna do this willy nilly all the time. You're going to have a set schedule. So every Tuesday we do our allocations and that means that somebody literally on my team goes into my bank account and moves the money into the separate accounts.

items.caption: Oooooo I could talk about Profit First for the rest of my life and never get bored because it changed my life by improving my business finances and my personal finances. @mikemichalowicz #cleaners #smallbusiness #cleaning
items.ownerFullName: Morgan Graffis | Cleaning Business Coach | Hiring & Growth
items.transcript: This is essentially the concept of profit first. You have your sales, which in other words is your revenue. So let's say you have $1,000 a day in revenue. That's what your clients pay you. So you have $1,000 of revenue, then you're going to subtract your profit, then that's how much you can allocate to your expenses. So what do we normally see? How is this any different? We normally see sales minus expenses equals profit, right? So normally in business, you'll have this equation to just see how much your profit can be. So this is what you're solving for. That's not what profit first says. So this is not the equation that we're using anymore. So instead of having your revenue minus all of your expenses that randomly come out and that you don't know how much it needs to be, and it just is what it is, instead of having your sales minus all of that stuff equals whatever this number may be, you're going to choose your profit, right? You're going to account for your profit first. So you're going to have your revenue, and then you're going to decide how much you can take out for your profit, and then the rest is what you can allocate to expenses. So your expenses aren't this thing that takes away from your profit. No, your profit needs to come first in this equation to make sure that you have a specific percentage that you always hold back for profit because that is what you prioritize. The expenses in your business, so think any overhead expenses, any storage units, any supplies, any products, anything, anything that's an expense in your business, this dictates this. So your revenue minus whatever your profit percentage is dictates how much you have to spend on your expenses, not the other way around. The original equation that many people use is your revenue or your sales minus your expenses dictates your profit, but that leaves your profit to be variable and unpredictable and not really up to you. But what you want is for your profit to be up to you. You don't want it to be in question what your profit is going to be, and you'll see when we go into how to find these percentages, so how to find like, okay, what is my profit percentage, Morgan? How do I actually figure out how much I can hold back? We'll get into that, but you'll also see that it's not just profit that you're putting first, it's your own owner's pay.

items.caption: How to actually get your cleaners to clean the same way for every house, every time #cleanersofinstagram #cleaners
items.ownerFullName: Morgan Graffis | Cleaning Business Coach | Hiring & Growth
items.transcript: The most important thing is as an owner, you just need to come to a conclusion as to what your standard operating procedure is for everything. That is the one thing that will absolutely like kill your entire training system for newbies because your trainers will all do it differently. They'll all get a slightly different result. They'll teach it differently. Your trainees will be confused and it's a mess. We don't want that. So we want one streamlined document where it lists how you do everything. And that how you do everything should be super clear. So once you have that done, as the owner of the company, you need to make sure that that is updated. The way that we're actually going to implement this is by making sure that all of your trainers have been trained properly on all of these SOPs. If you're the trainer, you need to make sure you know all of the SOPs. This is again, something where it's done on site. So if you're training a trainer on how to clean, you're not going to have this document out. You're just not. You don't need this document out. You're going to be standing side by side with the trainee, right? And you're going to be explaining how to do a fiberglass tub or how to clean a vent. You're not going to have your computer out looking at how to word it. But you need to make sure that the way that you do train it aligns perfectly with how you put it in this document. If you're struggling to explain how to do something, you can come into this document and control F. Let's just say tub. So you can control F showers and tubs, right? So once you control F, that's just like control find. You can search a word and you can come down here and you can see, okay, fiberglass. How do I clean a fiberglass? Okay, we're going to use these tools. These are the chemicals and this is the procedure. So you can kind of read through here. If you're struggling to train on something, you've just noticed that you're like, you're just like tripping up on how to explain how to do it. You can go in here in your off time, whether before you start a clean or after you start a clean, like after you finish the clean, I should say. You can go in here and just familiarize yourself with the language used on how to explain how to do these things. The most important thing honestly about this is that the owner lands on an SOP for every single thing in the house or every single thing in a commercial property. That's the most important thing.

items.caption:
Slow to catch on trainees in a cleaning business 🤓

#cleaners #cleaningcommunity
items.ownerFullName: Morgan Graffis | Cleaning Business Coach | Hiring & Growth
items.transcript: Repeating the same mistakes over and over again or just like struggling to recall stuff, you're making things too complicated. Stop complicating them. You're over-explaining things. You're giving too much information at once. Dumb it down for lack of a better term. Make it simpler. A good example of this is if you're standing in front of a shower with a trainee, right, and it's got glass, it's got tracks, it's got copper fixtures, it's got stone, maybe it's like pebble and grout, and you are standing there with the trainee and you're like taking 10 minutes to explain how to do the shower top to bottom. You're including every element of it. They're not going to remember and then they get nervous and they clam up and it's, don't do that. You're over-explaining. Break it down into smaller chunks and make your explanation super short. If you're doing a complicated shower, just explain the glass. Explain the glass. Have them start doing the glass. You start doing a different element of the shower if it's like a big enough space. If not, just explain the glass. You start doing something else. Once they're done with the glass, you start on how to do the fixtures. Maybe that's what we do. And then you start explaining. Okay, once they're done with the fixtures, you start explaining spot cleaning the grout. Then you're like, okay, so really with the way that this shower is now, the only thing we need to do is scrub the bottom and wipe it out. Whatever your flow is, only teach one thing at a time and go in the order that you need to, you know, whatever that shower looks like or whatever your process is.

items.caption:
What to do when a trainee is going to slow 😝

#cleanersofinstagram
items.ownerFullName: Morgan Graffis | Cleaning Business Coach | Hiring & Growth
items.transcript: If a clean should take five hours and it takes seven hours, then we have the wrong pace. So remember that pacing doesn't actually mean like how fast you're moving your body. It means that you're making the right micro decisions while you're cleaning something to make sure that it doesn't take you 30 minutes when it should take 10. Maybe it's the case that we are cleaning a toilet and see that, okay, the only thing that's on here that's, you know, built up is obviously the inside of the bowl. And then there's like dog hair everywhere. Probably shouldn't be the case that my first step is douse the toilet, right? Because then I'm like, I'm chasing the hair. It's taking me longer. It's taking me way longer than it should, right? So you should be making micro decisions as you're cleaning every single item that you're touching to make sure that you're as efficient as possible. It does not mean that you always have to move your body faster. Now, you should go at a professional pace when it comes to how fast you move your body as well. So don't get me wrong on that. But you should not be like sweating to death by the end of a clean. And this goes for your trainee as well. If your trainee is making up for the wrong judgment calls on each thing that they're cleaning by going too fast, it's going to burn them out. So they're going to be like making these weird judgment calls. Exactly the same thing I was saying. Let's say it's the toilet. There's a bunch of dog hair on there, but otherwise it's like pretty clean. It's just this house has a lot of dogs, right? So you start dousing the toilet when all the dog hair is on there. It's going to take you 10 minutes to wipe the outside of the toilet instead of two, right? Well, now the trainee is making those wrong decisions. You're not catching it. And they're only making up for it by moving their body faster. So then they're going to burn out. They're going to hate their job. And they're going to wonder like, how the heck are we supposed to get this done in five hours? Because you start bringing up time to them and then they start getting resentful. And it's this weird dynamic. We want to avoid that altogether. So you are in charge as the trainer to make sure that they are pacing correctly, not just how fast they're moving their body, but with those micro decisions to make sure that they're going at the right pace for each and every item that they're cleaning by making the right judgment calls.
